source.title: ZiCo: Zero-shot NAS via Inverse Coefficient of Variation on Gradients
source.authors: Gui-Hong Li; Yue-Dong Yang; K. Bhardwaj; R. Marculescu

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices. Some equations and figure labels are garbled by text extraction, but the relevant experimental descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper empirically relates gradient statistics to training and test loss, using a different measure from the claim versions' specific sharpness, memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, or example-removal tests.
record.gate_note: The MNIST experiments report trends between gradient statistics and training or test loss; these results concern the claim's broad topic but do not test any listed version's specific measure. NAS-benchmark proxy correlations and architecture-search accuracy comparisons do not measure the versions' stated behaviors.
record.test_reason: The study measures gradient-statistic associations with loss and evaluates a NAS proxy; neither tests any listed version. Its sharpness argument uses a Gram-matrix eigenvalue bound, not V7's magnitude-scaled weight perturbations or generalization-gap rankings. Varying batch sizes does not establish V5's large-batch performance penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors argue that gradient mean and standard deviation inform convergence and generalization, and that combining them in ZiCo yields useful accuracy rankings and efficient architecture search. Their generalization interpretation rests on theoretical bounds and test-loss associations, rather than direct measurements of generalization gaps or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical gradient-statistic experiments use MNIST linear and ReLU models and compare gradient statistics with loss; they do not reproduce the listed versions' interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The supplementary MNIST test-loss experiment varies batch size (64, 128, 256); the paper reports the same qualitative lower-standard-deviation/lower-test-loss tendency across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher squared mean-gradient sums accompany lower training loss in linear MNIST models; smaller gradient variance or standard deviation accompanies lower training loss and, for ReLU MLPs, lower test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient statistics track early training and test loss in the tested MNIST regression models.

record.problems: The MNIST gradient-statistic results are described as qualitative trends from figures without numerical estimates or uncertainty. They do not directly measure the train-test gap, and the paper's proxy benchmark correlations are not tests of the listed claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results were omitted. Benchmark proxy correlations and architecture-search comparisons are excluded because they report proxy ranking or search performance, not a result on one of the versions' specified behaviors.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under the specified tuning and training recipes.
Large-batch held-out performance penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery through recipe changes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation recipes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness versus generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, including comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states concern the listed claim versions; they do not deny the reported gradient-loss associations. Section 3.2.2 assumes a broader flatness-generalization relationship, but does not test V7. The omitted NAS comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out and supply no additional qualifying results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; held-out accuracy under random versus natural labels.
Test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under different tuning or weight-decay recipes.
Large-batch generalization gaps under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Effects of dropout and its removal on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Effects of removing memorized training examples on test accuracy.

rows.subject: linear model
rows.operation_detail: Compared total training loss after one update with the square sum of mean gradients across training samples.
rows.measure: Total training loss versus square sum of mean gradients.
rows.value: Networks with higher square sum of mean gradients tended to have lower training loss.
rows.note: The text states the trend; precise plotted values are not available in the supplied extraction.
rows.check: The reported association with training loss is supported, but it cannot determine any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: linear model
rows.operation_detail: Compared total training loss after one update with the square sum of gradient variances across training samples.
rows.measure: Total training loss versus square sum of gradient variances.
rows.value: Networks with lower square sum of variance tended to have lower training loss.
rows.note: The text states the trend; precise plotted values are not available in the supplied extraction.
rows.check: The statistic is the sum of gradient variances, Σσ_j², rather than the square sum of variances. Its association with training loss cannot determine any listed version.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP with ReLU
rows.operation_detail: Related gradient standard deviation across batches to training loss after one epoch.
rows.measure: Training loss versus gradient standard deviation across training batches.
rows.value: Networks with lower gradient standard deviation tended to have lower training loss.
rows.note: The paper also says lower gradient standard deviation tended to accompany lower test loss in this experiment; see R4.
rows.check: The training-loss association is supported but measures none of the listed versions. The model follows Eq. 7's regression setup with the second-layer weights fixed.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP with ReLU
rows.operation_detail: Related gradient standard deviation across batches to test loss after one epoch.
rows.measure: Test loss versus gradient standard deviation across training batches.
rows.value: Networks with lower gradient standard deviation tended to have lower test loss.
rows.note: No numerical values or explicit train-test gap are reported for this relationship.
rows.check: Test loss versus gradient standard deviation does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or the train-test gap. Figure 2(b) supports the reported association; the accompanying prose mistakenly cites Figure 2(a).
